newsitem.title: ITALY: EU's Monti urges Italy to redouble EMU efforts.
newsitem.headline: EU's Monti urges Italy to redouble EMU efforts.

text.p: European Commissioner Mario Monti urged Italy on Friday to step up its efforts to be ready for planned Economic and Monetary Union by deciding on a mini-budget and bringing forward a key pension review.

Monti told Corriere della Sera newspaper in an interview that Italy should decide swiftly on a mini-budget to be certain it will meet key entry criteria including a deficit-to-Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ratio of three percent.

"I think at this point it would be wise to be on the safe side so as not to run the risk of missing the three percent target in 1997," he said, adding Prime Minister Romano Prodi should not wait for outstanding data before making up its mind.
Prodi has said no decision on a mini-budget would be taken until state accounts are finalised, probably in March.
Monti said Italy should also speed up a review of its generous pension system. "It's hard to see why we don't bring things forward to 1997 since it's a key year," he said.

A controversial review of a landmark 1995 pension reform deal is not due until 1998 but Prodi wants to begin early. Unions and Communist Refoundation, the hard-left party that is a key government ally, are vehemently opposed.

EU states will be judged early next year on their fitness for EMU, which is due to start in 1999. Italy is determined to be a founder member and passed a tough 1997 budget to slash 62.5 trillion lire off this year's deficit to try to make the grade.
Official figures released last week, however, showed the 1996 deficit was well above target at 138.5 trillion lire, making a supplementary budget probably.
Monti said Italy could draft its 1998-2000 economic plan early -- it is due by mid-year -- to show it meant business.
"The sooner Italy shows its commitment to having a deficit for 1998 and subsequent years comfortably below three percent, the more credible will be its efforts towards EMU," he said.
Monti was in Rome on Friday and was due to attend a seminar on the Schengen accord, which creates a borderless Europe, together with Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano.
Italy has signed the accord but has lagged behind implementing all the measures needed to become a full member. It hopes to become a full member this year.
